title: Planning your plot — Beds and paths continued
status: Rejected by John; retain as trial history
review: The invented gardens looked AI-generated. Use John's real allotment for finger paths and research photographed working gardens for the remaining layouts.
setting: An invented Cornish demonstration garden: a low stone wall, timber gate at rear left, weathered shed and dark water butt at rear right. The pictures show alternatives for one patch at the same scale and from one viewpoint.
layout: Two parallel dead-end routes enter from the near edge, leaving continuous soil at the rear.
One spine from the near edge with two pairs of gently angled side branches. All tips end in soil.
prompt:
Create a matched pair of photographic illustrations for a UK vegetable gardening manual, presented as ONE wide landscape diptych, canvas aspect ratio about 2.4:1. Exactly two equal landscape photos touching at the centre, no white divider, no text, no lettering or arrows. Each half is an independent outdoor photograph of exactly the SAME invented modest Cornish kitchen garden, from precisely the same elevated spot and in the same soft spring daylight. They are two alternative planting layouts for one plot, not two neighbouring beds, nor two adjoining halves of one panorama. Think two exposures from one locked practical camera on a raised mast pointing steeply down about 65–70 degrees from horizontal. No horizon or sky. Left and right panel must each show the entirety of the ONE main growing rectangle, all four corners, continuous perimeter path and the garden landmarks. Let the plot occupy about 80% of each photo's width and 70% height so it reads at book size. Fixed frame, orientation, shadow direction, plants' approximate sizes and scale. No people.

Most important: REFERENCE 1 is the exact connectivity of the paths (tan is walkable, brown is soil, green is outer surroundings; NOT colours to copy literally). Reference 2 is the existing book drawing showing the SAME two alternatives and suggesting modest crop types. Rebuild them as real HUMAN-SCALE full-size domestic gardens from a camera, with actual foot-worn paths. Follow reference 1 for shape. Each is one rectangular patch roughly 4 m across and 3 m deep; no boards around the soil, no tall raised beds. The walkable internal routes are wide enough for a gardener to stand in, with tan, somewhat trodden woodchip aged to tawny brown and straw grey. Natural uneven mulch at path edges, level with the slightly mounded, deep brown crumbly tilth. Real, varied rows of fairly young vegetables, e.g. butterhead lettuce, beetroot with dark red stems, spinach, spring onions, no oversized crops. Don't hide the path openings or tips with plants. A few smooth stones, foot wear, blotchy natural lawn beyond, individual seedling leaves catching light. Avoid showroom perfection, surreal miniatures, 3D render, toy plants, floating island, artificially orange woodchips, embossed diagram or decorative parterre.

Left photo = TWO FINGER PATHS. A horizontal path along the near/bottom edge opens directly into two parallel straight walk-in dead ends, one at one-third width and one at two-thirds width. The two fingers run about three-quarters of the way back. Both terminate in the soil and leave a clear UNBROKEN planted band across the rear. No interior cross-connection, no central spine, no second entrance from the rear. The single planted area is continuous around both dead ends.

Right photo = LEAF-VEIN PATH. A single open central entrance from the NEAR/bottom perimeter leads into one main straight central spine, stopping in soil before the back boundary. Two PAIRS of short walkable side paths branch off the spine successively, angling gently forward to left and right like the veins of a leaf. Four short angled dead ends in total (two on each side). They connect only to the spine; terminate well inside the planted soil. Rear, left and right soil margins must stay continuous. No extra parallel fingers, cross-through to outer paths, closed loops, separate islands, or leaf-shaped outer border. One main rectangle same as first.

Identifiable shared setting: a low, weathered local stone wall defines the FAR boundary beyond the plot, a simple timber garden gate in the back LEFT corner of both photos, an understated partial corner of a muted natural timber shed with a dark rain butt on the back RIGHT beyond the bed in both. Only glimpses, just enough to locate us, kept in a narrow rim at top right; the vegetable plot must dominate. Small realistic house garden rather than an estate. Perimeter woodchip path wide enough to walk, continuous round the bed, with worn short grass beyond; no built frames. Preserve believable adult gardening scale in shed, gate, crops and paths. Clear spring daylight through thin cloud. A documentary photograph of a real spring afternoon with the same human-scale garden alternatively set out two ways. No graphic overlays, no names, no initials, no dimensions.
refinement: Retouch this specific photographic pair with extreme fidelity to the paths. Keep the exact 2.4:1 diptych, same background in the two independent photos, all boundaries, walkable path widths, locations of paths and the dead ends. The subject of this picture is the path geometry. Preserve two straight finger paths in the left plot. Preserve one central spine with four diagonal branches in the right plot. The tan side arms on the right all clearly stop short of the left and right perimeter; increase the strip of visible soil at each tip just enough that the eye unambiguously sees the dead end. Preserve the same modest Cornish kitchen garden, timber gate in upper left, rain butt at rear right. IMPORTANT improvement is NATURALISM AND SCALE of the vegetables: the existing one-giant-plant-per-dot planting and exposed red beet balls look like nursery display props. Change the crops inside the soil to realistic productive small-group planting. Reduce the size of most individual plants to about half, especially beetroot. The path is genuinely 45 centimetres wide and a young lettuce is ~12 centimetres across. Within the beds cluster three to six leafy young red-stemmed beetroot plants in a staggered short row, roots buried, no red spheres sticking above the ground. Put in a few short irregular rows of modest-sized young green and bronze loose-leaf lettuce clustered by variety, a little spinach and spring onions as unassuming background crop. Softer less yellow greens, some variation in leaf size and angle. Allow a few small soil gaps where germination missed. Show rich brown worked granular soil, an occasional garden pebble and gently feathered path margins. Keep all crops low; plantings must not obscure, interrupt or bridge any internal path. No new route, dividing board or landscaping. Make photographs look candid real editorial horticultural photography on a mild spring day, realistic small shoots and woodchip sizes relative to an adult-scale gate and shed rather than a model. The two panels should feel like you set out two alternative arrangements of the same ordinary plot, with the same practical mix of crops. No titles or callouts, no people.
